name: How I turned my room into a Virtual Pool Hall using a phone and Scrcpy
content:
A touchscreen would've made this better

Buying a 9-foot slate pool table requires two things I don't have: thousands of dollars and a massive spare room. But laying a spare monitor flat on a coffee table and wiring up an Android phone? That's basically free, and it turned out way better than it had any right to.

Mobile pool games like 8 Ball Pool are fun, but playing them on a 6-inch phone display strips away all sense of scale and perspective. You're just staring straight down at a tiny glass rectangle, pulling back a digital cue with your thumb. I wanted to see if I could recreate the feeling of standing over an actual table, gauging angles with real line-of-sight.

The stack for this was stupidly simple. I laid a desktop monitor horizontally flat on a small coffee table, hooked it up to my laptop, and plugged my Android phone in via USB-C.

To mirror the display with zero latency, I ran scrcpy over an ADB connection and pushed the window full-screen onto the flat monitor:

Once it was up, the dynamic completely changed. Instead of looking at a phone UI, you’re standing over a lit table surface. Lining up bank shots and lining up cue angles feels intuitive because your physical eyes are looking down at the board from above—just like real pool. Plus, unlike a physical table, you can swap out custom felt patterns, dark-mode tables, and neon arcade borders on the fly.

Wired ADB meant input lag was virtually non-existent, so fine adjustments were surprisingly crisp. The only real limitation is that you're still using the phone in your hand as the touch controller, meaning you occasionally glance down at your hands to adjust a shot rather than touching the table directly.

Slapping a large touch overlay onto the monitor would make it 1:1 with an arcade cabinet, but for a late-night weekend hack made out of desk clutter, it’s easily one of the most fun experiments I’ve built.

name: I created the definitive PSP AdHoc experience using 128mb of RAM
content:
Still less RAM than a modern browser tab

Setting up PPSSPP netplay with friends used to be a massive headache. If you've ever tried it, you know the drill: someone creates a virtual LAN network on ZeroTier or Hamachi, everyone scrambles to align their IP settings, and you spend twenty minutes arguing over who has the most stable connection to host. Half the time, the host-handshake drops anyway.

Since I already run a home server for self-hosted tools and game servers, I decided to fix this once and for all by spinning up a dedicated 24/7 AdHoc Server. No VPN subnets, no host juggling — just launch the game and play.

Instead of defaulting to Debian, I picked Alpine Linux for its tiny memory footprint and as an excuse to test out the distro. The installation was straightforward—I set export BOOTLOADER=grub during setup to stick with GRUB.

My first attempt was compiling and using Souler’s ppsspp-adhoc-server source code, but I soon ran into a limitation the original PSP had.
AdHoc on the PSP expected all the devices to be on the same network, which meant that Souler’s ppsspp-adhoc-server was doing dumb-routing and handing every connected client each other's IP addresses without verifying if the IP is correct or reachable.

To tackle this, I decided to switch to Kethen's aemu_postoffice and aemu AdHoc server, which is a reimplementation of the original AdHoc server paired with a relay server written in Node.js to rectify the dumb routing issue.
It fixes the issue by brokering the same network packets as the AdHoc server, but it modifies each packet to include the correct public IP of the device that is reachable over the internet, which we tell PPSSPP to prefer over the packets with incorrect IPs sent by the AdHoc server.

Setup was much simpler as both the AdHoc and relay servers were two single executables and had precompiled binaries available on GitHub, although it was quite confusing to track down the required files.
After sourcing the files, setting them up on my VM, exposing a few ports and making some changes to my PPSSPP clients, I was able to finally connect to my server from outside the network without any hiccups.

Once it ran cleanly, I wanted the VM to feel like a dedicated server rather than just another anonymous VM. I configured tty1 to autologin a separate adhoc user, then made a script into its home directory that starts both services and set it to autorun on login, making the whole thing autonomous.

Now every time the VM boots, the script draws a custom system header using fastfetch with a bright yellow credit banner, and fires up the server binaries on ports 27312 and 27313.

The server now seamlessly bridges players over both my local LAN and the open internet. The whole VM uses just about 45 MB of RAM and boots in 4 seconds. Games like Ridge Racer and Test Drive Unlimited run without a hitch — zero setup friction, rock-solid latency, and a server footprint so light my host machine doesn't even notice it's there.
